newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH SUPREME COURT HEARS JAILED TAPIE'S PLEA.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH SUPREME COURT HEARS JAILED TAPIE'S PLEA.

text.p: France's Supreme Court began hearing a plea for a retrial on behalf of bankrupt former tycoon and soccer boss Bernard Tapie on Tuesday after the fallen ex-cabinet minister spent his first night in jail.
Tapie was not in court to hear his lawyer make a last bid for the Cour de Cassation to quash his conviction for rigging a 1993 soccer match when he was chairman of the Marseille club.

If the court rejects his plea, Tapie will have to serve an eight-month sentence for bribery and interfering with witnesses over the fixing of a Marseille-Valenciennes First Division match a few days before Tapie's club won the 1993 European Cup.

The 54-year-old rags-to-riches businessman, who is still a Radical member of the European Parliament, evaded waiting cameras when he turned himself in to prison authorities on Monday evening after a final day of suspense.

Hidden under a blanket in the back of his son's car, he was driven to the Quai des Orfevres police headquarters, where he was put into an anonymous white prison transport bus with frosted windows and taken to La Sante prison in central Paris.
Prisoner number 265 449 G, incarcerated on his own in a freshly-repainted nine-square-metre cell of the prison's VIP wing, was the top story in all French newspapers on Tuesday.

Reporters chronicled his farewell to his family as if he were King Louis XVI embracing his children before being taken to the scaffold, rather than a convicted fraudster going to serve a short sentence after exhausting all legal recourses.

One of Tapie's lawyers, Emmanuel Piwnica, told Reuters he would argue that a lower court had had no right to sentence Tapie to prison while he was still a member of the French and European parliaments. He has since been stripped of his French seat and is due to lose his European seat on February 17.
He said he would also challenge the legal classification of the offences as "corruption" and "interfering with witnesses".
The Supreme Court may give its verdict immediately or adjourn for a few days' deliberation. If the Court rejects his appeal, he will remain in prison.

However, under French law he should be entitled to serve most of his sentence at an open prison, spending the nights in a cell and being allowed out in the daytime to work in his new profession as a cinema actor.
Tapie's longtime conservative political rival for Marseille city hall, Urban Affairs Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin, voiced sympathy for his fallen adversary on Tuesday.
"It's a terrible ordeal for Tapie today. Going to jail is always an ordeal and I don't wish it on anyone," Gaudin, who is also mayor of Marseille, told France Inter radio.
